title: ADKAR: Diagnose Before You Train
headline:
CHANGE STARTS
WITH A PERSON.
need: A Nike client-program team is adopting a new quality-review workflow. The training lead must discover why an employee is not yet using it before assigning more training.
outcomes: Distinguish the five ADKAR outcomes in workplace evidence.
Select support that fits the earliest unmet outcome in a fictional case.

concepts.title: Awareness and Desire
concepts.body: Awareness concerns why the change is needed. Desire concerns a person’s willingness to participate. A person may understand the business reason and still have a concern that affects participation. Listen for the difference.

concepts.title: Knowledge and Ability
concepts.body: Knowledge concerns what to do and how. Ability concerns putting that knowledge into practice. Someone may explain a process but still need guided rehearsal, time, access or coaching to carry it out.

concepts.title: Reinforcement
concepts.body: Reinforcement helps the changed behavior continue. Look for follow-up, feedback and recognition tied to the new way of working. Do not assume a launch announcement or course completion creates sustained adoption.

concepts.title: Use evidence, then check again
concepts.body: ADKAR is Prosci’s model for individual change. It is not a complete change methodology. Use conversations and observed work to locate an early unmet outcome, propose support and revisit the evidence. These original scenarios are not Prosci’s proprietary assessment.

example.title: A new quality-review workflow
example.body: Jordan explains why the workflow matters, wants to use it, and correctly describes the steps. In a practice case Jordan cannot apply the rubric consistently, despite having system access.
steps: Awareness and Desire have supporting evidence.
The observed performance gap points to Ability.
Offer coached practice with feedback, then observe another case.

practice.prompt: Mina says, “I know how the new process works, but nobody has explained why we need it.” What should you investigate first?
practice.feedback: Start by clarifying the need for change and listening to the concern; another how-to course does not answer the stated question.

draft.prompt: A colleague supports a new process and can explain it, but cannot complete a practice case unaided. Write a support plan and the evidence you would check next.
draft.label: Your support plan
draft.model: Investigate the Ability barrier through observation. Provide a coached practice case, remove access or tool obstacles, then observe an independent case using the agreed criteria.
criteria: Uses evidence rather than a personality label

quiz.prompt: “Why are we changing?” most directly signals a question about…
quiz.feedback: The statement asks about the reason for change.

quiz.prompt: A colleague understands the need but does not want to participate. Investigate…
quiz.feedback: Understanding the reason and willingness to participate are different outcomes.

quiz.prompt: A willing colleague cannot describe the required steps. Which support fits?
quiz.feedback: The case suggests a Knowledge need; first check that earlier outcomes are supported.

quiz.prompt: A colleague explains the steps but struggles in practice. Which response fits?
options: Coached practice and removal of performance obstacles
quiz.feedback: Ability requires demonstrated performance, not just explanation.

quiz.prompt: People performed the new behavior, then reverted. What should you examine?
options: Reinforcement and the conditions sustaining the behavior
Whether ADKAR is a software system
quiz.feedback: Follow-up should investigate the environment and reinforcement, while checking for new barriers.

jobaid: Ask what evidence supports each outcome.
Look for the earliest unmet outcome.
Match the support to the barrier.
Observe again; do not equate attendance with adoption.

creative.headline:
CHANGE STARTS
WITH A PERSON.
creative.context: Nike client-program lens · Training & quality leadership
creative.role: You are the training lead supporting a fictional client-program process change. Listen to the employee, identify evidence of a barrier, and choose proportionate support.
creative.answer: A useful success statement is observable: each open ticket has an owner and a next action before the shift ends. Tool installation alone is not adoption.

transcript:
Fictional Cedar Service is replacing email handoffs with a shared ticket queue. The desired behavior is specific: before ending a shift, each coordinator assigns every open ticket to an owner and records the next action. Installing the tool does not establish that behavior.

Prosci’s ADKAR model concerns individual change. Its five elements are Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability and Reinforcement. In brief: understand the reason; choose to engage; learn what to do; demonstrate it; keep it going. The model is one part of a wider change-management approach.

This sample uses original conversations to explore those distinctions. It is not an official diagnostic instrument. Treat a possible barrier as a hypothesis to discuss, rather than a score that defines someone.

Worked example: a coordinator can explain the new handoff steps but has never completed them in the live workflow. You have some evidence of knowledge. You do not yet have evidence that the person can carry out the behavior in realistic conditions. Record exactly what you observed before choosing a response.
